studies.label: Normandy
studies.title: Which missions made a difference to the ground advance?
studies.answer: Reconnaissance gave the armies a picture of the Dives crossings. Photographs later showed a rail line cut at Bourth. At Cobra, a much larger bombardment helped open the way, but infantry and armour still had to fight for the roads to Marigny and Saint-Gilles.

points.title: What the ground staff could learn
points.text: On 16 July, No. 430 Squadron RCAF reported roughly twelve Dives bridges intact despite poor visibility. On 22 July the 416th Group’s report on Bourth cited photographs showing breaks in the railway track. The photographs confirm damage at Bourth. The Dives reconnaissance concerned other crossings six days earlier.
points.locator: Mission 103, results and later photographs. Dives observation in the evidence table below.

points.title: What the ground forces still had to do
points.text: On 26 July VII Corps sent its mobile units forward to deepen the penetration. Their commanders had expected the roads to be clear and instead put assault troops up front. The 416th had dispatched the same number of aircraft to support the advance on two successive days. It recorded a bombing pattern at Saint-Gilles on the first day and cloud preventing the Marigny attack on the second.
points.locator: Chapter XIII, pp. 251–253. Missions 105 and 106 identify the group’s own results.

studies.label: Battle of Britain
studies.title: What kept fighter squadrons available for the next raid?
studies.answer: Fighter Command drew down its reserve of replacement Hurricanes and Spitfires. At Northolt, repairs put nine Polish squadron Hurricanes back into service overnight. Aircraft supply, pilot strength and the number a squadron could launch on a given call each tell a different part of the story.

points.title: The reserve available for issue
points.text: On 10 August the maintenance units could issue 160 Hurricanes and 129 Spitfires to Fighter Command. By 7 September they could issue 86 and 39. The same study reports that Fighter Command considered itself 201 pilots below authorized strength on the latter date.
points.locator: Battle of Britain chapter, aircraft supply around fig. 3-3 and Pilot and Aircraft Resources.

points.title: Two squadrons at Northolt
points.text: After the fighting on 15 September, No. 303 Squadron’s ground crew restored nine damaged Hurricanes for the following day. On 27 September No. 1 RCAF scrambled twelve, then eight, then six aircraft. Those launches show repeated commitments through a single day. The sources do not trace the Canadian aircraft individually.
points.locator: Ground personnel after 15 September. Canadian scramble counts in the RCAF timeline below.

studies.label: Defence of the Reich
studies.title: What could the 445th Bomb Group fly the day after Gotha?
studies.answer: The 445th lost thirteen of its twenty-five dispatched Liberators at Gotha on 24 February. The following day it dispatched seventeen to Fürth. Twelve reached the primary target. The two mission reports establish next-day capability even though the aircraft and crews that made it possible have yet to be matched.

points.title: A second mission after severe losses
points.text: The Fürth return records seventeen takeoffs and dispatches, five aborts and twelve aircraft over the primary target. Counting the whole group on both days avoids attributing the wider Eighth Air Force loss total to the 445th.
points.locator: Mission 29, group table under Fürth, 25 February. The preceding Mission 28 covers Gotha.

points.title: What one defending unit could still launch
points.text: III./ZG 26’s diary traces launches from Wunstorf on 20, 21 and 24 February. Four aircraft took off on the 24th and the diary recorded a Liberator claim. Matching that claim to a 445th aircraft would require a time, location and identified loss on both sides.
points.locator: Kogler diary, III. Gruppe entries for 20, 21 and 24 February.

studies.label: Operation Bagration
studies.title: What did Soviet air concentration change around Bobruisk?
studies.answer: The 16th Air Army assembled 526 aircraft for one evening strike against the trapped German force. German-side records place the closing of the pocket before the attack. Aviation added pressure on an already encircled army, and the same air army went on to support the advance toward Baranovichi.

points.title: Order of events matters
points.text: Ziemke’s account traces Ninth Army’s delayed retreat orders and the Soviet ground forces closing the pocket on 27 June. Its sequence changes what can be credited to that evening’s air strike. Bombers, assault aircraft and fighters attacked a force whose routes out had already narrowed.
points.locator: Chapter XV, The Bobruysk Pocket, 26–27 June.

points.title: What remained available
points.text: The 16th Air Army reported 769 sorties around Baranovichi on 7 July. The Bf 109G-6 inventory of III./JG 51 fell from forty at the start of June to twenty-four at its close, then sixteen at the end of July. Both series show forces continuing to operate as the front moved, but one counts flights and the other aircraft held.
points.locator: Bf 109G-6 movement return, June and July. The 7 July sortie figure comes from the Soviet air-army history.

studies.label: Malta and Sicily
studies.title: When did fighters delivered or moved forward actually supply protection?
studies.answer: Malta’s May 1942 receiving arrangements put newly arrived fighters into service within 35 minutes. During the Sicily invasion the next summer, fighters covered the beaches before an island base was ready. The move to Pachino then put a named squadron in a position to keep patrolling and to cover ships off Syracuse.

points.title: Arriving, surviving and flying
points.text: After Calendar’s April delivery, raids struck the airfields while Spitfires were on the ground. For Bowery on 9 May, teams were prepared to service the arrivals. The RAF entry records 134 fighter sorties that day across the defence. The source does not assign all those flights to the newly delivered aircraft.

points.title: What reached the harbour
points.text: Five of Pedestal’s fourteen merchant ships reached Malta in August, including the tanker Ohio. Malta Command recorded about 32,000 tons of general cargo, alongside separate furnace-fuel and diesel quantities. The convoy documents how supplies got through while the escorts and island fighters opposed attacks. The cargo total cannot measure aviation fuel issued to fighter squadrons.
points.locator: August 1942, Malta Command war diary, outstanding events and unloading of Ceres.

points.title: What a patrol supplied
points.text: On 13 July 1943 eleven pilots left Luqa, patrolled the beaches and landed at Pachino. No. 92 recorded five patrols there on the 14th and eight aircraft covering ships on the 16th. Its diary names Rodney and Nelson. Nelson’s naval chronology places her Catania bombardment later than the diary does. The patrol itself is well documented.
points.locator: No. 92 Squadron Form 540, 13–17 July. Both accounts are available in the linked Sicily campaign record.

studies.label: German replacement capacity
studies.title: Why did new aircraft fail to restore German fighter strength?
studies.answer: German aircraft acceptances remained high while fighter units faced shortages of pilots and fuel. In April fewer replacement pilots arrived than the fighter force reported losing. Over the summer the fall in aviation gasoline output forced further reductions in training and even in the time allowed to run in engines.

points.title: What the unit returns show
points.text: Murray’s table for Luftflotte Reich counts 472 operationally ready single-engine fighters on 1 June and 242 on 1 July. The proportion ready actually rose slightly because the command’s holdings also shrank. The snapshots describe a single command during deployments to the invasion front.
points.locator: Chapter VII, table LIX and discussion of dispositions in June.

points.title: What fuel shortages changed
points.text: The Strategic Bombing Survey found that curtailed fuel supply cut pilot training further. In August the final engine run-in was reduced from two hours to half an hour. Its national aircraft acceptance figure, 39,807 in 1944, includes all types. It provides industrial context without telling us how many fighters a particular command could fly.
points.locator: Aircraft and Oil sections, especially printed pp. 6–9.

points.title: Factories kept delivering into 1945
points.text: The monthly all-type series records 3,188 aircraft in January, 2,249 in February and 1,930 in March. It establishes continued output during the collapse. Neither a fighter-unit allocation nor an airworthy aircraft with a trained pilot can be inferred from these totals.
points.locator: Vol. VII, table I.I.10, p. 118, derived from USSBS report 2a. Published table transcription, pending check of the underlying monthly scan.
